explain.say: A hard, green, sour fruit turns soft, colourful, sweet and smelly. Ripening is the plant's way of saying: my seeds are ready, come and eat me.

explain.say: Many fruits, like bananas, apples and tomatoes, start ripening by making a gas called ethylene. It acts as a hormone, switching on all the ripening changes and drifting to nearby fruit too.

explain.say: Stored starch turns into sugar, so the fruit gets sweeter, while sour acids fade. Enzymes loosen the glue between the cells, so the fruit softens.

faq.a: Ethylene is a simple gas that plants use as a hormone. It triggers ripening, and because it is a gas, one ripening fruit can set off its neighbours.

faq.q: Why does a ripe banana make other fruit ripen faster?
faq.a: Ripe bananas give off lots of ethylene. Put an unripe avocado or pear in a paper bag with a banana and the trapped gas speeds up its ripening.
asks: How can I ripen fruit faster?

faq.q: Why does fruit ripen at all?
faq.a: Ripening makes fruit tasty and easy to spot just when the seeds inside are mature. Animals eat the fruit and spread the seeds, often far away, in their droppings.

faq.q: Why are unripe fruits sour and hard?
faq.a: Unripe fruit protects seeds that are not ready yet. It is full of starch and acids, and sometimes bitter chemicals, which put animals off eating it too soon.

faq.q: Do all fruits keep ripening after picking?
faq.a: No. Bananas, apples, tomatoes and avocados keep ripening after picking because they make ethylene. Grapes, strawberries, cherries and oranges barely ripen once picked, so they are harvested ripe.

facts: Ethylene is a gas that acts as a plant hormone and triggers ripening in fruits such as bananas and tomatoes.
Fruits that keep ripening after picking, such as bananas and avocados, are called climacteric fruits.
Fruit is often shipped in cool stores with controlled air to slow ripening on the journey.
